scenes.visual: Reuse the first film's exact dark slate canvas (#0F172A), 'schematic' tag, and colour map: teal receptor cell (#2DD4BF) above, amber ligand cell (#F59E0B) below, clasped across the cleft with teal forward and amber reverse arrows glowing. Bold white title 'Which Direction Did the Work?' appears over the cleft and fades at 1.8 s while the cells stay.

scenes.tts: In the first film, a membrane ligand signaled inward through a tail or partner. Now suppose you delete that ligand's gene and an organ fails to form. How can you tell which direction caused the defect? One knockout removes too much at once.
scenes.caption: In the first film, a membrane ligand signaled inward through a tail or partner. Now suppose you delete that ligand's gene and an organ fails to form. How can you tell which direction caused the defect? One knockout removes too much at once.
scenes.visual: Same two-cell contact world (teal cell above, amber cell below, schematic). The amber ligand's tail glows briefly to recall the first film, then a slate 'Delete ligand gene' stamp dissolves the amber ligand completely. A small schematic organ icon at screen right dims and fragments, while large '?' badges pulse over both the teal and amber cells.
scenes.narration: In the first film, a membrane ligand signaled inward through a tail or partner. Now suppose you delete that ligand's gene and an organ fails to form. How can you tell which direction caused the defect? One knockout removes too much at once.

scenes.tts: Watch what vanishes when you delete the ligand gene completely. First, the receptor cell loses its forward signal. Second, the ligand cell loses its reverse signal. Third, both cells lose the physical grip holding them together. Deleting the receptor gene creates the exact same tangle.
scenes.caption: Watch what vanishes when you delete the ligand gene completely. First, the receptor cell loses its forward signal. Second, the ligand cell loses its reverse signal. Third, both cells lose the physical grip holding them together. Deleting the receptor gene creates the exact same tangle.
scenes.visual: Three live status bars sit cleanly beside the cleft (font >= 28 pt): 'Forward' (teal), 'Reverse' (amber), 'Grip' (white). As the amber ligand vanishes, all three bars switch off one by one in sync with speech, and the two membranes drift apart. The amber ligand restores briefly, then the teal receptor vanishes instead—and the exact same three bars switch off together.
scenes.narration: Watch what vanishes when you delete the ligand gene completely. First, the receptor cell loses its forward signal. Second, the ligand cell loses its reverse signal. Third, both cells lose the physical grip holding them together. Deleting the receptor gene creates the exact same tangle.

scenes.tts: To separate bidirectional signals, disable one inner route while keeping binding. Leave the outer binding tip on the cell surface so the two cells still grip. Then cut or swap only one cell's intracellular signaling part, keeping the other side intact.
scenes.caption: To separate bidirectional signals, disable one inner route while keeping binding. Leave the outer binding tip on the cell surface so the two cells still grip. Then cut or swap only one cell's intracellular signaling part, keeping the other side intact.
scenes.visual: Restore both proteins clasped across the cleft so all three status bars are on. A clean schematic dashed cut line trims ONLY the teal receptor's inner kinase domain inside the upper cell, leaving the teal outer binding tip clasped tightly to the amber ligand. The 'Forward' bar switches off, while 'Reverse' (amber) and 'Grip' (white) stay brightly lit.
scenes.narration: To separate bidirectional signals, disable one inner route while keeping binding. Leave the outer binding tip on the cell surface so the two cells still grip. Then cut or swap only one cell's intracellular signaling part, keeping the other side intact.

scenes.tts: Watch this rule solve a brain wiring puzzle. Growing axons carrying B type ephrins cross floor cells carrying the receptor eff B two. In mice lacking eff B two completely, those axons veer off course. A second mouse keeps eff B two's outer tip on the surface.
scenes.caption: Watch this rule solve a brain wiring puzzle. Growing axons carrying B-type ephrins cross floor cells carrying the receptor EphB2. In mice lacking EphB2 completely, those axons veer off course. A second mouse keeps EphB2's outer tip on the surface.
scenes.visual: Zoom out smoothly from the cleft into a cross-section of a developing brain tract ('Anterior commissure', schematic), keeping the exact colour map: a row of teal floor cells ('EphB2') beneath moving amber axon fibers ('Ephrin-B'). Split into two stacked lanes: top lane labelled 'No EphB2' shows teal receptors gone and amber axons veering downward off track; bottom lane labelled 'Outer tip kept' shows teal outer tips still anchored on the floor cells.
scenes.narration: Watch this rule solve a brain wiring puzzle. Growing axons carrying B-type ephrins cross floor cells carrying the receptor EphB2. In mice lacking EphB2 completely, those axons veer off course. A second mouse keeps EphB2's outer tip on the surface.

scenes.tts: In that second mouse, an inert bacterial enzyme replaces the receptor's inner kinase. That change removes the receptor's own kinase signal. Yet the axons still stay right on course. Pause and think: which cell was receiving the guidance signal?
scenes.caption: In that second mouse, an inert bacterial enzyme replaces the receptor's inner kinase. That change removes the receptor's own kinase signal. Yet the axons still stay right on course. Pause and think: which cell was receiving the guidance signal?
scenes.visual: Focus on the bottom lane ('Kinase-less EphB2'): inside the teal floor cells, the coral kinase block is swapped for a dull slate block ('Inert marker'), dimming the teal forward arrow to off. Amber axons glide smoothly straight across the teal floor cells, staying on course. A crisp white question card appears at the bottom: 'Which cell received the guidance signal?'
scenes.narration: In that second mouse, an inert bacterial enzyme replaces the receptor's inner kinase. That change removes the receptor's own kinase signal. Yet the axons still stay right on course. Pause and think: which cell was receiving the guidance signal?

scenes.visual: Deliberate thinking pause. Keep the two lanes visible (top: No EphB2 -> axons off course; bottom: Kinase-less EphB2 -> axons on course) with the question card 'Which cell received the guidance signal?' and subtle pulsing highlights alternating gently between the teal floor cells and amber axons over a 4.5 s bar.

scenes.tts: The axons carrying the ephrin received the signal, because the only working part left was the receptor's outer tip. That tip stayed on the floor cells and gripped the axons' ephrins, so the message ran inward there. Here the protein named receptor acted as the ligand.
scenes.caption: The axons carrying the ephrin received the signal, because the only working part left was the receptor's outer tip. That tip stayed on the floor cells and gripped the axons' ephrins, so the message ran inward there. Here the protein named receptor acted as the ligand.
scenes.visual: Question card fades. Bright amber reverse-signaling arrows light up inside the amber axons as their ephrins contact the teal outer tips of kinase-less EphB2 on the floor cells, while the slate inert blocks inside the floor cells stay dark. A crisp callout tag flashes above the teal outer tip: 'Acts as ligand', and inside the amber axon: 'Acts as receptor'.
scenes.narration: The axons carrying the ephrin received the signal, because the only working part left was the receptor's outer tip. That tip stayed on the floor cells and gripped the axons' ephrins, so the message ran inward there. Here the protein named receptor acted as the ligand.

scenes.tts: Mutant animals test whether one direction is needed. A second tool tests whether reverse signaling is enough on its own. Scientists fuse a receptor's outer tip to an antibody handle, making a soluble receptor body. With no receptor cell present, a response that needs the ligand must have entered through it.
scenes.caption: Mutant animals test whether one direction is needed. A second tool tests whether reverse signaling is enough on its own. Scientists fuse a receptor's outer tip to an antibody handle, making a soluble receptor body. With no receptor cell present, a response that needs the ligand must have entered through it.
scenes.visual: Return to the two-cell cleft world and slide the entire teal receptor cell completely off the top of the frame. Into the empty extracellular space float Y-shaped soluble blocks built from teal receptor outer tips joined to a slate antibody stem ('Receptor-Fc'). They dock onto amber membrane ligands on the remaining lower cell; only an amber downward arrow can appear, since no teal cell exists.
scenes.narration: Mutant animals test whether one direction is needed. A second tool tests whether reverse signaling is enough on its own. Scientists fuse a receptor's outer tip to an antibody handle, making a soluble receptor body. With no receptor cell present, a response that needs the ligand must have entered through it.

scenes.tts: For example, developing sympathetic axons carry uncut membrane T N F. Adding soluble T N F receptor one makes those axons branch more. That growth requires membrane T N F on the axon. If a protease cuts T N F loose, that inward link breaks. Released T N F can still float off and signal forward.
scenes.caption: For example, developing sympathetic axons carry uncut membrane TNF. Adding soluble TNF receptor 1 makes those axons branch more. That growth requires membrane TNF on the axon. If a protease cuts TNF loose, that inward link breaks. Released TNF can still float off and signal forward.
scenes.visual: Show an amber sympathetic axon membrane carrying three-stemmed amber membrane TNF blocks ('Membrane TNF', schematic). Teal soluble 'TNFR1-Fc' clusters dock onto uncut TNF -> amber reverse arrow lights up and the axon tip sprouts new branches. Then a slate scissor icon ('Protease') clips the outer amber trimer loose; the stub stays in the membrane with no reverse arrow inside, while the released amber trimer floats upward toward a distant teal receptor.
scenes.narration: For example, developing sympathetic axons carry uncut membrane TNF. Adding soluble TNF receptor 1 makes those axons branch more. That growth requires membrane TNF on the axon. If a protease cuts TNF loose, that inward link breaks. Released TNF can still float off and signal forward.

scenes.tts: Full knockouts erase forward signaling, reverse signaling, and cell contact all at once. Keep outer binding intact and disable one inner route at a time. Only then can you prove which cell received the message.
scenes.caption: Full knockouts erase forward signaling, reverse signaling, and cell contact all at once. Keep outer binding intact and disable one inner route at a time. Only then can you prove which cell received the message.
scenes.visual: Return to the clean two-cell cleft with the three status bars ('Forward', 'Reverse', 'Grip'). Show a quick side-by-side comparison: left, 'Full KO' (all three bars off); right, 'Targeted cut' (outer clasp intact, 'Grip' on, only one inner arrow disabled). The targeted side glows steadily as the full-KO side dims.
scenes.narration: Full knockouts erase forward signaling, reverse signaling, and cell contact all at once. Keep outer binding intact and disable one inner route at a time. Only then can you prove which cell received the message.
